components.text: The decisive demand is to justify applying classical singularity reasoning where quantum effects undermine general relativity.
The additional demand is to distinguish evidence against eternity from proof that the whole universe absolutely began.
Whether singularity-based beginning claims survive the failure of classical general relativity at quantum scales.
Whether the cited considerations establish an absolute beginning of the whole universe rather than only limited past finitude.
The decisive demand is whether BGV reaches the whole regress rather than merely the onset of inflation.
Whether BGV establishes only a beginning to inflation or also excludes an infinite regress of prior universes.
The decisive demand is to compare design with viable alternatives rather than assume a God-or-multiverse dichotomy.
Whether fine-tuning favors design when probability distributions are unknown and several non-theistic explanations remain available.
The decisive demand is whether the multiverse has evidential support despite the absence of direct observation.
Whether the multiverse lacks observational support and is therefore evidentially weaker than divine fine-tuning.
The decisive demand is a defended probability distribution and comparison with multiple non-theistic explanations.
The additional demand is to compare theism with the cited indirect predictive support for a multiverse.
Whether unknown probability distributions and multiple non-theistic alternatives undercut a design inference.
Whether the multiverse has indirect observable support that improves its comparative evidential position.
The decisive demand is whether Genesis appears ordinarily human because its cosmology contains ancient physical errors.
Whether Genesis is best explained as ordinary human ancient composition because of its alleged physical errors.
The decisive demand is whether the luminary language makes biblical cosmology distinctively accurate rather than ordinarily ancient.
Whether biblical treatment of celestial lights is sufficiently distinctive and accurate to count against ordinary ancient composition.
The decisive demand is whether solid-sky language defeats Scripture once its intended theological function is distinguished from scientific description.
The additional demand is to explain the alleged sequence, timescale, water, and firmament errors under the proposed genre.
Whether ancient physical imagery undermines revelation when the text's legitimate purpose is theological rather than scientific instruction.
Whether alleged physical errors retain decisive force once the Bible's intended theological genre and limited purpose are considered.
The decisive demand is to explain hundreds of millions of years of animal suffering before human beings existed.
The additional demand is to explain the scale and variety of natural and biblically attributed animal suffering.
How animal suffering for hundreds of millions of years before humans could have resulted from Adam and Eve's revolt.
Why the scale and distribution of natural and scriptural animal suffering are expected under a good redemptive God.
The decisive demand is to reconcile allegedly divine killing and scriptural violence with divine goodness.
The additional demand is to explain the existence of prehuman animal suffering before human sin.
Whether divine killing and scriptural violence conflict with the goodness and moral standards attributed to God.
Why prehuman animal suffering is compatible with divine goodness or results from human sin.
The decisive demand is to account for natural cruelty and suffering when inferring a good purposive creator.
Why extensive prehuman animal suffering should not count against a purposive and good creator.
Whether natural cruelty and extinction undermine selective appeals to natural beauty and order.
The decisive demand is whether beauty alone is representative evidence for a purposive and good creator.
Whether nature's beauty and order, considered as a whole, provide substantial evidence of purposive creation.
The decisive demand is whether brain-state evidence supports a sufficiently complete physical account of conscious experience.
Whether brain-stimulation and evolutionary evidence sufficiently support a physical account of phenomenal states.
